title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest spans your five tracked topics — anti-aging (drugs, topicals & devices), HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Highlights this morning: two new NIH-backed rapamycin trials, a JAMA Network Open biofeedback RCT, and the ASCO-presented DEDiCa lifestyle trial. Sources are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.topic: Anti-Aging — Rapalogs, Mitophagy Supplements & Exosome Topicals
sections.body:
The theme today: **serious longevity science is finally moving into well-controlled human trials**, while the topical/device space is getting interesting with exosome delivery.

- **Two new rapamycin (mTOR-inhibitor) trials launch.** The NIA-collaborating **RESTOR** study (*NCT06658093*, UT Health San Antonio) began recruiting in March 2026 to find the dose and timing of rapamycin/everolimus that safely restores "youthful" mTOR signaling in older adults — and it's explicitly powered to test whether the **optimal dose differs by sex**. Separately, the **University of Arizona** is starting a **$12M, double-blind Phase 3** of low-dose rapamycin in adults 65+, tracking the transition to frailty and the inflammatory marker **IL-6**. Bottom line: rapamycin remains the molecule with the strongest human *healthspan-relevant* signal, but there is still **no completed human lifespan trial** — these will help fill the gap.
- **Mitophagy supplements — where the human data actually is.** **Urolithin A** (which restores mitophagy) has two RCTs behind it, and an **NIH Clinical Center trial (*NCT06274749*)** testing 1 g/day on glucose metabolism and mitochondrial function in adults 55+ **began July 28, 2026**. **Taurine** and **NMN** remain promising but earlier-stage (strong animal/mechanism data; human outcome trials pending), while **resveratrol** has largely failed to reproduce in humans.
- **Topicals & devices — exosomes as a delivery vehicle.** A 12-week **randomized split-face RCT** (28 adults) found adipose-stem-cell **exosomes + microneedling** beat microneedling + saline on wrinkle roughness (12–14% vs 7% reduction), elasticity (+11% vs −3%), hydration and pigmentation, confirmed by histology showing more new collagen. A separate 2026 open-label study of a **biomimetic-exosome-encapsulated retinal** cream showed photodamage improvement with **less irritation than conventional retinoids**.

Practical framing: favor interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-supplement "longevity" claims skeptically. Most topical/exosome trials are still small and short — watch for larger, longer studies.

sections.body:
Fresh 2026 evidence reinforces HIIT as a **time-efficient** tool for women's cardiometabolic health — with a recurring nudge to **combine it with strength work**.

- **Postmenopausal women (new RCT).** A 2026 clinical trial (45 women 50–65 with overweight/obesity; *NCT07302191*) compared **12 weeks of HIIT vs. concurrent (aerobic + strength) training**, 3×/week. Both significantly cut body weight, BMI, abdominal fat, triglycerides, total and LDL cholesterol, glucose, insulin and **HOMA-IR** vs. controls. **Concurrent training** produced the *greater* drops in weight and body-fat %, while metabolic-marker improvements were similar — a strong argument for **adding resistance work** rather than doing intervals alone.
- **Middle-aged & older women (2026 meta-analysis).** A new systematic review of **19 RCTs (646 women, ages ~44–81)** found HIIT reliably improves **VO2max** (large effect, high certainty) with a borderline gain in walking ability. Notably, HIIT alone did **not** significantly boost muscle strength — again pointing to pairing it with resistance training.
- **Metabolic syndrome.** In menopausal women with metabolic syndrome, HIIT outperformed **moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)** for reductions in weight, BMI, body-fat %, waist circumference, triglycerides, insulin and HOMA-IR.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio and metabolic wins; **add strength training**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate. A blended week (HIIT + resistance) covers the most bases.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). This week's studies clarify *which* add-ons help and offer alternatives for women who can't isolate the pelvic floor.

- **Biofeedback: the *type* matters.** A multicenter **JAMA Network Open RCT** (452 women with postpartum SUI) found that adding a **home-based pressure-mediated biofeedback device** to supervised PFMT beat PFMT alone — cure rate **20.2% vs 8.7%**, larger drops in incontinence severity, and better muscle strength and adherence at 3 months. This contrasts with the large **BMJ EMG-biofeedback trial (600 women)**, which found **no difference** at 24 months. Takeaway: **real-time pressure feedback that reinforces daily home practice** may help, whereas clinic-only EMG biofeedback added little.
- **Can't feel the pelvic floor? Hypopressives are an option.** **Hypopressive exercises** — rib-cage expansion plus breath-hold (apnea) that *reflexively* co-activates the deep core and pelvic floor — keep showing benefit. A 2026 RCT (44 postpartum women) found 12 weeks of hypopressives **improved abdominal function, body image and pelvic-floor complaints** (though it did not close diastasis recti), and an RCT (*NCT07322328*) is directly comparing hypopressives vs. PFMT for postpartum SUI.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or a feedback tool, keep up daily practice, and consider hypopressives if voluntary Kegels are hard to perform.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" here is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard therapy** — not a replacement. Two themes stand out for HER2-positive (often TP53/p53-altered) disease.

- **A precision vulnerability in HER2;TP53 co-mutant tumors.** New preclinical work (mouse models + organoids) confirms that HER2-mutant tumors carrying **TP53 mutations** grow faster and are **resistant to neratinib**, yet stay **sensitive to the TOP1-inhibitor payload (exatecan)** inside **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd)** — because mutant-p53 tumors show high histone acetylation and hyper-transcribed DNA-repair genes that make them susceptible via G2/M arrest and apoptosis. The **neratinib + T-DXd** combination this predicts is now in a **Phase 1 NCI trial (NCI 10495, *NCT05372614*)** for HER2-altered solid tumors. Germline **TP53** mutations are also linked to early-onset HER2+ disease, so genetics matter in this group.
- **Lifestyle as adjuvant therapy (ASCO 2026).** The randomized Phase 3 **DEDiCa** trial (492 women) tested a high-intensity **low-glycemic Mediterranean diet + daily brisk walking + vitamin D** vs. standard advice. Overall recurrence didn't differ, but **hormone-receptor-positive** women who **adhered** to the full program had a **76% lower recurrence risk** (HR 0.24), plus far higher metabolic-syndrome remission (65% vs 34%) — benefit attributed to all three components together.
- **Supplements — mechanism vs. proof.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Oncology* review maps supplements (**curcumin, omega-3s, quercetin, resveratrol**, etc.), flagging **bioavailability limits** and real **herb–drug interaction** risk with targeted therapy. Repletion of **vitamin D** during neoadjuvant therapy has improved pathologic complete response in some trials, and the **NEOMET** trial (*NCT06928701*) is testing omega-3s + exercise added to neoadjuvant treatment.

Important framing: the co-mutant/T-DXd data is **preclinical + early trial**, and integrative diet/supplement evidence is mostly **observational or subgroup**. Use these as *add-ons discussed with your oncology team* — never substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy — and coordinate any supplement to avoid interactions.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance still puts **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **New AASM combination guideline (2026).** The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's clinical practice guideline on *combination* therapy issued two **conditional** recommendations: **CBT-I + medication** beats **medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I delivers durable improvement without drug risks. **No single drug** emerged as a preferred add-on. Start with **CBT-I**; add medication selectively and briefly for specific goals (e.g., short-term total-sleep-time gains).
- **Medications for fragmented sleep.** For sleep-*maintenance* (waking during the night), newer **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** — **lemborexant, daridorexant** (FDA-approved since the 2017 guideline) — are better tolerated with less next-day "hangover" than Z-drugs/benzodiazepines. Z-drugs remain best kept **short-term**.
- **Supplements — modest, honest expectations.** A 2025 double-blind RCT (155 adults) found **magnesium bisglycinate** (250 mg elemental Mg + glycine) produced a **small but significant** drop in Insomnia Severity Index at 4 weeks — largest in those with **low baseline magnesium** (a 2026 study found *no* notable effect, so response likely depends on your levels). A 2026 systematic review supports **L-theanine 200–450 mg** for calmer sleep onset without grogginess, and ~3 g **glycine** before bed has small-trial support. The AASM continues to recommend **against routine melatonin** for chronic insomnia (it's most useful for circadian issues like jet lag/shift work).

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room **cool, dark and quiet** (bedroom darkness has stronger evidence than any pill).
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disrupted sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
